newsitem.title: SWEDEN: H&M keeps Xmas undies ad under wraps.
newsitem.headline: H&M keeps Xmas undies ad under wraps.

text.p: Hennes & Mauritz's (H&M) Christmas underwear advertising campaign remains one of the most closely guarded secrets in Sweden's advertising world -- and usually one of the most controversial.
The Swedish fashion retailer's eighth annual Christmas campaign for women's underwear is due to be revealed this month and is expected, as usual, to star one of the world's top models.

But H&M's chief executive and controlling owner Stefan Persson has refused even to give any clues about who would appear this year in a campaign that has drawn both praise and virulent opposition since it first hit the streets.
"We don't want to give our competitors any clues about what we are doing," Persson told Reuters in an interview at his central Stockholm office.
H&M's advertising agency, Stockholm-based Ronnberg, was also tight-lipped about the campaign, its content and release date.
"We cannot release any information," said a spokeswoman.

The campaign sparked controversy in the advertising world when it started because H&M, which specialises in low-price, high street fashion in its 450 stores across Europe, decided to splash out and put top models in its undies.
Previous Christmas lingerie models include U.S. supermodel Cindy Crawford and Australia's Elle "The Body" McPherson.
The campaign has been so successful that H&M is now using the winning formula in other campaigns throughout the year, including its annual swimwear campaign.
"We think it is good to have a top model," said Persson, whose father, Erling, founded the company.
"It shows the difference and we are prepared to pay for it.
"We use professional, good models. We use professional, good photographers. We choose to have the best quality."
But the ads of scantily clad top dollar bodies have received mixed reactions, from feminists stealing the posters to burn them to men taking them home as souvenirs.
The first campaign in the series in 1989 started out on a dangerous footing.
Adverts plastered all over London Underground railway stations sparked a storm of protest because of the slogan: "What the au pair will be wearing this winter".
Britain's Advertising Standards Authority was inundated with complaints about the campaign and some Scandinavian women in London said they had received unwelcome attention as a result.
H&M countered the response running more ads, this time with the slogan: "Last time we ran an ad for Swedish lingerie 78 women complained; no men." It only sparked more protests.
H&M's swimwear ads have also been controversial.
Smash and grab thefts of posters featuring U.S. model Tyra Banks in Belgium earlier this year prompted the clothing retailer to organise free handouts of the pictures.
The campaign featured a bikini-clad Banks in a variety of poses on the 50th anniversary of the two-piece swimsuit.
A company spokeswoman said at the time the thefts had been a problem "but not as bad as last year when we had Pamela Anderson in a swimsuit".
In Sweden the campaign using Anderson, the busty, blonde star from the U.S. television series "Baywatch", caused a stir.
Protesters doused four of H&M's Stockholm stores with a foul-smelling liquid, described by witnesses as a cross between ammonia and vomit, to demonstrate against the adverts.
A letter to a Stockholm newspaper, signed by the previously unheard of Former Anorexics Fight Back, accused H&M of promoting the slimmers' disease anorexia nervosa in its campaign.
Model Anna Nicole Smith, Playboy magazine's former Playmate of the Year, was ruled a danger to road safety in Norway in 1993 when she appeared in a series of H&M posters.
The Norwegian parliament ruled that roadside posters of Smith advertising H&M lingerie were enough to distract even the most cautious driver and ordered the posters be taken down.
The Norwegian Equal Opportunities Council said the adverts featured "the biggest breasts ever seen on advertising posters".
But the company have countered charges of sexism with a campaign for mens' wear.
Top male model Marcus Schenkelberg was put into H&M boxer shorts for one winter undies campaign. No one complained.
